Borrowing and Deposit 6.about: When a watchman may pay instead of swearing; what a watchman's oath includes; a watchman's stipulation to guard less; deposits made before witnesses; and disputes over what was returned.

1.text: If the article is easy to buy, like plain produce, he may simply pay. If not, like an animal or a decorated garment, he first swears it isn't in his hands, since he may have wanted it for himself.

2.text: The watchman is believed that they agreed he would guard it less carefully, since he could have said it was lost by forces beyond his control. He swears to that, and to the other points.
2.term: Miggo: a claim is believed because the person could have made a better one.

4.text: With witnesses to this very article, the watchman can't claim he bought it. After his death, someone who gives clear signs gets it, if the judge knows the deceased was unlikely to own it and the claimant didn't visit often.

5.text: When the owner says the article returned is a different one, damaged, or less, the watchman takes only a sh'vuat hesset. If he admits part of the amount claimed, he takes a Torah oath.
5.term: Sh'vuat hesset: a lighter oath the Sages added, for claims the Torah's oath doesn't cover.

Borrowing and Deposit 7.about: Entrusted produce that spoils, and when to sell it; caring for scrolls and garments; using entrusted money; moving an entrusted jug; deposits from women, servants and children; where a deposit is returned; a watchman who must travel.

1.text: Normal shrinkage: he leaves it alone. More than normal: he sells it through a court, to kohanim at the price of terumah, in case the owner had made it terumah.
1.term: Terumah: the portion of produce given to a kohen, which only a kohen may eat.

4.text: All this care applies only when the owner is overseas. If he is in the same land, the watchman doesn't touch it, even if it is being ruined.

6.text: Sealed or specially tied money he may not use, so he isn't liable if it's lost or stolen. Money just bound in a bag he may use, so he is a paid watchman: liable for loss or theft, not for armed robbers.

9.text: Moved for his own needs: he is liable if it breaks, even after he put it back. Moved for the jug's sake: he isn't, even if it broke after he set it down somewhere else.

11.text: The owner may claim it only where he deposited it, but must accept it if the watchman returns it elsewhere, unless it was deposited in a settled place and brought back in the desert.

Borrowing and Deposit 8.about: Who receives the thief's double payment when a watchman pays instead of swearing; profits that come by themselves; cases the Talmud leaves unresolved; and claiming from the thief.

1.text: A watchman who chose to pay rather than swear gets the thief's double, or four or five times, payment. If he swore instead, it goes to the owner. The animal itself, with its wool and young, goes back to the owner.

2.text: Each of these watchmen earns the double payment by admitting he must pay, when another claim would have freed him. A borrower earns it only once he actually pays.

3.text: If he paid willingly, a later rise in value is his. If the court had to force him to pay, the article goes back to the owner, and his money, goods or land go back to him.

5.text: In each of these the Talmud leaves the law unresolved, so the double payment or the gain is split between owner and watchman. Whoever seizes it all first keeps it.

6.text: Even after swearing, an unpaid watchman may choose to pursue the thief; a paid one must. If a stolen animal is returned and then dies through his negligence, he doesn't pay, but the owner keeps what he seizes.

Forbidden Foods 13.about: Wine stored in a gentile's courtyard; wine kept pure for a gentile; leaving wine with a gentile under seals; safeguards the Sages added; and money from gentile wine: wages, debts, partnerships and sales.

1.text: If the Jew lives in that courtyard, the wine stays permitted even with the door open, since the gentile fears he'll walk in. If he lives elsewhere, he locks it and keeps the key and seal.

3.text: Here the wine is the gentile's, so a Jew's key and seal don't help: only a guard living in the courtyard keeps it permitted. The gentile wouldn't fear being caught, since at worst he loses the sale.

15.text: Money from selling most forbidden things is permitted, but not from idolatry or libation wine. The Sages treated ordinary gentile wine the same, so even wages for working with it are forbidden.
15.term: Stam yeinam: ordinary gentile wine, not known to have been poured to an idol, which the Sages forbade.

21.text: If the gentile sold them on his own, the money is permitted. If the Jew agreed to wait for it, it is forbidden, since he wanted those things to stay, so as to be paid from them.

23.text: Price set first: the gentile is committed before he touches the wine, so the money is from permitted wine. Measured first: his touch forbids the wine before the sale is settled, so the money is forbidden.

25.text: Paying the storekeeper in advance makes the Jew the buyer of whatever the worker takes, so it is as if he bought him libation wine.

3: ואם היה השומר דר בחצר אחרת

Creditor and Debtor 1.about: The mitzvah to lend to the poor; not pressing a debtor who can't pay, and the borrower's duty to repay; how a court collects a debt; what is left for the debtor.

3.text: A lender may not even pass by a debtor he knows can't pay, so as not to shame him. And a borrower who has the money may not put him off, nor waste the loan.

4.text: Movables are taken first, then land. Land already pledged to a ketubah or an earlier creditor is still given to this lender, but the earlier claimant may later take it from him.
4.term: Ketubah: the marriage contract, which pledges the husband's property for a sum due to his wife.

5.text: The weekday clothes of his wife and children, even new ones bought for them, stay theirs. Shabbos and festival clothes, and any jewelry, go to the creditor.

7.text: He keeps food for 30 days, a year of clothes fitting for him, bedding, sandals, tefillin, and two of each tool of his trade. Oxen, a donkey or a ship are property, not tools, so they are sold.

8.text: Movables his wife took to live on while he is away go to the creditor, since even he couldn't support his family before paying his debt.

Creditor and Debtor 2.about: A debtor who has nothing: the Torah's law and the oath the Geonim added; when that oath isn't given; guarding creditors against collusion; lending only before witnesses; loans from a servant or a wife.

2.text: No one may enter the debtor's home. Because cheats grew common, the Geonim added a severe oath: he owns nothing beyond what he is left, hid nothing, and will give the creditor all he earns beyond his basic needs.

4.text: The oath is only for cheats. A debtor known to be poor and honest isn't made to swear; one known as a cheat isn't allowed to, and is pressed to pay if the court can.

6.text: Reuven's admission that Levi's note is unreal or paid can't cancel Shimon's right to it, since they may be scheming together. Shimon swears and collects from Levi.
6.term: Shtar amanah: a note written on trust, before any money was actually lent.

Creditor and Debtor 3.about: Collateral: never from a widow, and never utensils for making food; taken only through the court, standing outside; returning what a poor debtor needs; what the court's agent leaves; guarantors and unpaid wages.

4.text: Only the court's agent may take collateral by force, and even he waits outside. A creditor who took it himself isn't lashed if he gives it back; if it was lost or burnt first, he is, and its value comes off the debt.

5.text: A poor debtor gets back what he needs when he needs it: the pillow by night, the plow by day. Collateral taken when the loan was given needn't be returned at all.
5.term: Sh'mittah: the seventh year, when outstanding loans are cancelled.

6.text: The agent leaves his clothes, eating utensils and a bed. Of two of a kind, one is returned. What he doesn't need is held 30 days, then sold through the court.

Forbidden Foods 14.about: The olive-sized measure for forbidden foods and what counts toward it; eating bit by bit; eating in a way no one enjoys; when danger to life permits forbidden food, and which comes first; one bite under several prohibitions.

4.text: The size counts as it is when eaten: shrunk below an olive's size, there is no punishment; swollen back, there is. Smaller from the start and then swollen: forbidden, but no lashes.
4.term: Kerait: being cut off, a punishment from Heaven.

8.text: Small bites add up if the whole olive's size was eaten within the time it takes to eat a p'ras. Over a longer time they don't, even with no pause between bites.

11.text: Eating it in a way no one enjoys, scalding, raw fat, made bitter or spoiled, brings no punishment. Meat with milk and mixed species of the vineyard are the exception, since the Torah forbids them even without enjoyment.

12.text: Eating idly still counts, since he enjoyed it. A pleasure that comes to him against his will is permitted, unless he intends it.

17.text: The lighter prohibition comes first: nevelah before tevel, which carries death by Heaven; Sabbatical-year produce, forbidden only by the Sages, before either; tevel before terumah, if it can't be fixed, since it isn't holy.
17.term: Tevel: produce from which terumah and tithes haven't yet been separated.

19.text: Each new prohibition here adds something, to benefit, to the altar, to his own eating, to all food, so each one takes hold despite the one before it.
19.term: Me'ilah: using consecrated property for oneself.

Creditor and Debtor 4.about: What interest is, and the prohibitions it involves for lender, borrower and everyone involved; returning it; heirs and repentance; extra money found; coins that change; waiving interest; orphans' money.

3.text: There are no lashes, since the interest must be given back. Fixed interest, forbidden by the Torah, is taken back through the court, though not from the lender's heirs.

4.text: Heirs needn't return interest money, but must return a specific item, for their father's honor, if he had repented before he died.

10.text: An extra amount one could easily miscount, like 1, 2, 5 or 10, is returned. A larger one is taken as a gift, or as stolen money quietly returned.

11.text: If the coin was made heavier and prices fell because of it, the increase is deducted. If prices didn't fall, he pays in current coins, unless the increase was more than a fifth.

13.text: Some Geonim held that a borrower can't waive interest. The Rambam disagrees: he may waive it, like stolen money, as the Sages' teaching about not accepting repayment shows.

Creditor and Debtor 5.about: Interest with gentiles: the Torah's law and the Sages' limits; passing such loans between Jews; guarantors and converts; investments that favor the investor; interest paid before or after, even in words; things like interest; ways around it.

2.text: The Sages limited lending to gentiles at interest to what one needs for a living, so as not to learn from their ways. Borrowing from them is fine, and a Torah scholar may lend for profit.

3.text: A Jew can't take over another Jew's interest-bearing loan from a gentile. The gentile must take his money back and lend it to the new borrower himself.

6.text: Interest owed to a gentile who converts: collected if added to the loan before he converted, otherwise not. Interest owed by a gentile who converts is collected in full, so no one says he converted to escape it.

8.text: Investing so that the investor gains much and risks little is the shade of interest. If it was done, profit and loss are shared as in an iska.
8.term: Iska: one person's money traded by another, with profit and loss shared.

15.text: Selling wheat for a maneh and buying it back for 90 is allowed in itself, but the Sages forbade it as a way around interest. If done anyway, the full 100 is collected.

Creditor and Debtor 6.about: Interest the Torah forbids and interest the Sages forbade; living in a borrower's courtyard; an asmachta; sales with a promise to return; fields given as security, the three kinds, and the Geonim's view.

1.text: Any agreed increase on a loan, like a free stay, cheaper rent, or a pledged property already producing, is Torah interest and taken back by the court. Anything else is the Sages' shade of interest, which isn't.
1.term: Asmachta: a commitment made on a condition one doesn't expect to happen, so it isn't binding.

2.text: Living there free without an agreement is the shade of interest, so he should pay rent. If it comes off the debt, the judges decide how much, since the court can't take back the shade of interest.

4.text: "If you don't repay in three years, it's mine" is an asmachta, so the produce comes off the debt. "It's yours from now if I don't repay" works: repaid within three years, no produce; after, all of it.

6.text: Part paid: each eats produce by his share. "From now, once you pay": neither eats, and a third party holds it. "Once you pay": the seller eats. "From now, the rest is a debt": the buyer eats.

7.text: A courtyard, bathhouse or store gives benefit right away, so using it is fixed interest. A field may or may not produce, so it is only the shade of interest. With a yearly deduction, a field is permitted, a courtyard isn't.

8.text: These Geonim forbade all security without a deduction, allowing it only as a rental: a set term after which it returns free, or a set rent deducted whenever he repays.

Forbidden Foods 15.about: Forbidden food mixed with permitted: taste for a different kind, a majority for the same kind, and the Sages' measures of 60, 100 and 200; what is never cancelled; how the measure is reckoned; taste that spoils; roasting and salting.
heads: When a trace forbids it all

1.text: A different kind forbids the mixture if its taste comes through. The same kind can't be tasted, so by Torah law a majority of permitted food cancels it.
1.term: Bitul: a forbidden thing cancelled by a larger amount of permitted food.

3.text: Torah lashes need an olive's size of fat in each three eggs' worth eaten. With less than that, or with only the taste, there are only the Sages' lashes.

6.text: Libation wine and tevel aren't cancelled at all in their own kind. In a different kind, taste decides, as with everything else.

10.text: Anything that will become permitted later, like new grain after the omer or muktzeh after the festival, is never cancelled, even in thousands, since there is a way to permit it.
10.term: Muktzeh: something set aside, not for use on Shabbos or a festival.

13.text: Terumah and the like are cancelled in 101, and a se'ah is taken out for the kohen. In less, the whole mixture becomes meduma.
13.term: Meduma: a mixture with terumah in it, which only a kohen may eat.

17.text: Most Torah prohibitions are cancelled in 60. The gid's fat is measured the same way, though only the Sages forbade it, since the gid is a creation of its own. The gid itself gives no taste.
17.term: Gid hanasheh: the sciatic nerve, which may not be eaten.

25.text: One may not add permitted food on purpose to cancel a Torah prohibition. If he did, it is permitted, but the Sages forbade it to him alone, as a penalty.

32.text: A goat roasted in its fat is all forbidden, since the fat spreads through it. If lean, with fat about one in sixty, he cuts and eats until he reaches the fat. Sinews give no taste, so they are just cut away.

Creditor and Debtor 7.about: Fields given as security: settling up when the lender leaves, custom on when he can be removed, and what follows from it; selling the land to the lender; higher rent for later payment; trading work; paying workers in advance.

1.text: Even if he ate produce worth the whole debt, he isn't sent away with nothing, since that would be collecting the shade of interest by force. With orphans' land he is, and two notes are counted as one.

3.text: Local custom decides whether the borrower may repay early and remove him. A clear stipulation overrides the custom, but a lender who agrees to leave early, against the custom, must confirm it with a kinyan.
3.term: Kinyan: a formal act that makes a commitment binding.

4.text: Where he can be removed at any time, the field isn't really his: his creditors can't take it, a firstborn gets no double share of it, and the Sabbatical year cancels the debt. Where he can't, the opposite.

9.text: A loan to improve the rented field, store or ship is permitted for higher rent, since the property is now worth more. A loan to trade with, or to hire sailors, is forbidden.

11.text: Trading the same work, weeding for weeding, is fine. Different work, or summer plowing for winter plowing, is not, since plowing in the rainy season is harder.

12.text: Paying in advance for later work at a lower wage looks like a loan repaid with cheap labor. If the work starts today, it is permitted.

Creditor and Debtor 8.about: A higher price for later payment, and a discount for paying early; selling dearer while the seller keeps the risk; buying fruit before it ripens; wages in cheap wheat; extra given freely; renting with wear; tzon barzel; returning interest paid in goods.

3.text: Selling for double with payment later is allowed if the seller keeps the risk until it's sold, or the buyer may return what he can't sell at a profit.

6.text: He must till under the vines, which makes it like buying the tree for its branches. Otherwise his money is a loan, repaid with cheap branches.

10.text: Here the buyer takes the risk of the price, so it can bring gain or loss. Wine that soured was already going to sour, so he may return it.

12.text: The owner shares the gain but the shepherd bears the loss, so it is the shade of interest. If the owner keeps the risk of price changes and predators, it is permitted.
12.term: Tzon barzel ("iron sheep"): sheep whose value is guaranteed, as if made of iron.

Creditor and Debtor 9.about: Paying now for produce delivered later: only once a market price is set, or when the seller has the goods nearly ready; which market price counts; ordering at the lower price; agents; buying from villages and travelers.
heads: When an order may be placed

1.text: Once a market price is set, one may pay now for later delivery at that price, even if the seller has none, since others do. A seller who already has the goods may sell before the price is set.

2.text: One or two steps from ready counts as having it; three or more counts as not having it at all.

3.text: Selling whatever he will milk or shear, however much it is, is fine. A set amount at a set price is forbidden, unless it is at the market price.

5.text: Paying at today's price, one may agree to get the lower price if it falls. Without that, he gets the price of the day he paid. An agent's buyer gets the lower price, or the money back.
5.term: Mi shepara: a curse pronounced on one who backs out of a deal after the money was paid.

6.text: Selling cheaply for later delivery is allowed only if he has wheat now. Wheat others owe him still has to be collected, so it counts as none.

Forbidden Foods 16.about: What even a trace forbids: leaven, spices, and important things that are never cancelled; living animals; mixtures that mix again; forbidden things that help cancel each other; orlah shells as dye and fuel; cheese; libation wine in mixtures.

2.text: Forbidden yeast or spice enough to leaven or season the food forbids all of it, even at one in a thousand.
2.term: Orlah: the fruit of a tree's first three years, forbidden even for benefit.

5.text: A forbidden piece among thousands forbids them all, since a piece one serves to guests is important. Once it is taken out, the rest needs sixty times its size.

10.text: A pomegranate from the forbidden mixture that falls into two others is cancelled by the majority, so one from that second mixture forbids nothing further. Falling into a thousand, it forbids them all.

11.text: Once these are cracked, cut or opened, the usual measures apply: 201, or 60 for minced meat.

13.text: Neither yeast alone could leaven the dough, but together they do, so an Israelite may not eat it. A kohen may.

16.text: If the dough was already leavened or the pot seasoned, ask whether the forbidden yeast or spice could have done it alone. If yes, all is forbidden; if not, the usual measures apply.

19.text: One forbidden thing can help make up the amount that cancels another. Once something is cancelled, the whole mixture counts as permitted.

22.text: Baking while the orlah fuel's fire is still there forbids the food, since the forbidden wood improved it. Once the fire is raked out, the heat left is permitted.

28.text: Pouring onto a drop of libation wine forbids it all. Poured slowly from a small bottle into a cistern, each drop is cancelled as it falls; from a big jug, the stream joins them, so all is forbidden.

34.text: Wheat absorbs the wine, so taste can't test it. It may be used for benefit, but sold to a gentile only as bread, which a Jew won't buy back.
